brief-1.text: False dichotomy: keep the overnight rota as it is and keep losing vets, or close overnight to protect staff. Third option: separate night work from day work with dedicated night vets or night-only contracts, so day vets stop doing nights on top of their normal rota. The burnout comes from nights stacked on day shifts under the equal-share policy, and supply exists: the group turned down an experienced emergency vet last spring because she only wanted nights. The salient clue, exit interviews blaming 'nights', points toward closing.

False dichotomy: a fully staffed clinic from 7 pm to 8 am, or no overnight service. Third option: keep the clinic staffed until about 1 am, when 71% of overnight patients have arrived, and cover the under-two-a-night load after that with phone triage and a vet on call from home, as the farm team already works.

False dichotomy: keep the overnight clinic or lose the four dairy contracts (about EUR 260,000 a year). Third option: change or close the small-animal overnight clinic and leave farm calving cover untouched. Calvings are attended on the farm by the farm-animal vets on their own home rota, and they have never used Kilbride at night, so the contracts do not depend on the clinic. A reply that counts the EUR 260,000 as a cost of closing has missed this.

False dichotomy: Fernlea absorbs the EUR 190,000 loss alone, or it closes. Third option: a shared out-of-hours arrangement with Thornby Vets, whose clients are about a fifth of overnight patients and which runs no out-of-hours service of its own. Thornby could pay a fee or retainer, or put its vets on the rota.

brief-2.text: False dichotomy: a popular-classics season, or keeping the 38% arts council grant. The grant condition counts works by living composers across the season, not concerts or whole programmes, so Ilse's reading ('a fifth of our concerts' as contemporary programmes) overstates it. With 16 concerts of three or four works each (about 50 to 64 works), roughly 10 to 13 works by living composers is enough. A short piece by a living composer in each popular programme meets it, and existing works count, so it does not require EUR 35,000 commissions.

False dichotomy: popular repertoire and music by living composers treated as opposites. The only main-stage sell-out was a concert of film and video-game scores, all by living composers, so a regular strand of that work fills the hall and counts toward the grant. The salient clue, Ilse dismissing it as 'not real repertoire', points away from it.

False dichotomy: the main stage carries either the orchestra's artistic identity or its ticket sales. Third option: make the players' Unbound foyer series the main home for adventurous new music. It sold out all six nights with a much younger audience, so the main stage can lean more accessible while the players' artistic outlet grows, which speaks directly to the principal players' threat to leave.

False dichotomy: one programming direction for the whole season. The weakness is concentrated in the Saturday single-ticket concerts (48% full), while the Friday subscription concerts average 81%. Third option: reprogramme Saturdays as the accessible series and largely keep the Friday series' character.

brief-3.text: False dichotomy: remove all engineers' production database access, or leave access as it is. The audit finding names standing write access only, and the CISO's plan to remove all access goes further than the finding. Third option: remove standing write access and keep read access, ideally through a replica or masked views. That closes the finding without blinding engineers.

False dichotomy: engineers stay in the production ledger, or support loses sight of transactions. 91% of the 14,200 sessions were SELECT-only status lookups for customer tickets. Third option: a read-only support lookup tool or replica that covers these needs without production ledger credentials.

False dichotomy: raw write access for fast incident fixes, or slow incident response. 29 of the 38 Sev-1 fixes were one of three recurring statements: re-queue a payout batch, release a settlement lock, correct an FX rounding row. Third option: build these as audited, parameterised admin or runbook actions that on-call can run in minutes without database write access.

False dichotomy: standing access, or just-in-time grants that are too slow at 3 am. Third option: keep just-in-time access and fix its speed. Use the existing proxy's time-limited, logged grants for the rare remaining writes, and pre-authorise the on-call engineer to self-grant instantly (break-glass), with automatic logging and review afterwards. The salient clue, Anders's complaint about speed, points toward rejecting the proxy.
